To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

higher positive affect (PA), which is the feeling that one is experiencing a positive emotion such as happiness, predicted lower externalizing symptomatology over time, but only for those adolescents with poor neural prefrontal functioning (indexed by lower hemodynamic response during the cognitive interference task), which is an important part of the brain for cognitive control.
higher positive affect (PA), but not higher negative affect, predicted lower internalizing and externalization symptomatology.
higher levels of positive affect predicted decreases in externalization symptoms over time, but only among adolescents with poor neural, not behavioral, prefrontal cognitive control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that emotion plays in the development of adolescent psychopathology and how cognitive control influences the relation between emotion and adjustment.
the role of positive affect in adolescent development and adjustment, and the role of cognitive control in this process.
the role of cognitive control in emotion–behavior relationships and its implications for adolescent adjustment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of emotion regulation on adolescent adjustment is dependent on cognitive functioning.
the findings indicate that positive affect is related to a decrease in externalizing problems, but only for those adolescents with poor cognitive control.
the findings of the present study are consistent with the notion that positive affect is a beneficial emotion for adolescents with poor pre-frontal functioning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cognitive control moderates emotion–symptomatology relationships.
positive emotions are not always good and that they may have different effects depending on the individual's cognitive functioning.

the effects of positive and negative affect on internalizing and externalization problems are moderated by prefrontal functioning, and that the effects of prefrontal functioning on the development of internalizing and externalizating problems may be moderated by affective states.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cognitive control may be one of the mechanisms through which emotion impacts adolescent adjustment.
positive emotions can be beneficial for adolescents with poor pre-frontal functioning, but not necessarily for adolescents with better pre-frontal functioning.
the effects of positive affect on adolescent internalizing or externalizing problems are not uniform, and are dependent on prefrontal function.
